content: Middle age is defined as the stage of life that follows young adulthood but precedes old age. It is generally considered to occur during the third quarter of the average human lifespan, typically between the ages of 40 and 60. Some definitions extend this range slightly, with the U.S. Census including individuals aged 35 to 54, while Erik Erikson defines middle adulthood as spanning from 40 to 65 years. In many Western societies, this phase of life is often associated with a sense of stability in identity, career, and family life. It is also a time when individuals may experience the onset of a mid-life crisis. During middle age, visible signs of aging become more apparent. These include a loss of skin elasticity and the graying of hair. Physical fitness tends to decline, with many individuals experiencing a 5-10 kg (10-20 lb) increase in body fat, reduced aerobic capacity, and a decrease in maximal heart rate. Strength and flexibility also diminish over time. However, the rate of aging varies significantly among individuals, even those of the same chronological age. Female fertility declines markedly after the age of 40, and advanced maternal age increases the likelihood of certain conditions in offspring, such as Down syndrome. Similarly, advanced paternal age is associated with an increased risk of some disorders in children. Most women undergo menopause in their late 40s or 50s, marking the end of natural fertility. In developed countries, mortality rates begin to rise from age 40 onward, primarily due to age-related health conditions such as cardiovascular disease and cancer. Despite this, the majority of middle-aged individuals in industrialized nations can expect to live into old age. In contrast, life expectancy in developing countries is significantly lower, and the risk of death at all ages is higher. Some individuals challenge the notion that middle age is a period to be feared. They argue that, with a positive mindset and careful planning, middle age can represent the most fulfilling years of a person’s life. Age-positive groups, ranging from advocacy organizations like the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) to social clubs such as the Red Hat Society, promote this perspective.
